ideas.statement: Test the atlas's strongest structural claim — the perfect complementary distribution of destination (S6) and preamble (S9) — against pre-modern and early-modern chancery instruments in which a named addressee and a recital coexist (royal letters patent, chancery mandates, farmans addressed to named governors), to determine whether the epistolary/normative fork is universal or an artefact of modern codification.
predicted_observations: `[prediction]`:
Pre-modern addressed instruments with recitals produce a non-zero S6×S9 "both present" cell, weakening the perfect negation to a strong but imperfect tendency.
The co-occurrence concentrates in source-tradition genres whose name means "command/letter to a person" rather than "edict to no one."
Modern standards-era systems retain the perfect negation — i.e. the fork's scope is historical (a modern regularity), not universal.

`[prediction]`: A pre-modern sample of ≥30 dated instruments across ≥3 chancery traditions with S6×S9 both-present = 0 would leave the fork intact and kill the challenge; single counterexamples with ambiguous coding also fail to disconfirm (threshold: recurrence in ≥2 traditions).
uncertainties: `[assumption]`:

The 14-slot vocabulary maps onto pre-modern instruments without distortion (the atlas already codes the 1412 Islamicate scroll, so medium-flexibility is assumed, not proven for addressed medieval genres).
Open, citable transcriptions/translations of pre-modern instruments are obtainable by one researcher without a consortium.
A single coder's S6/S9 judgments are reliable enough that a *pattern* of co-occurrence (across ≥2 traditions, not scattered single cells) would be visible.

`[assumption]`: Linguistic coverage for one person (Latin/Old French, Ottoman Turkish or Arabic, possibly Ge'ez) and dependence on published translations, which may blur the recital/addressee distinction; ~3–5 weeks of manual coding; CPU irrelevant; no participants, no ethics review.

ideas.statement: Build a small longitudinal panel by sampling the same chancery lineage at four or more dates (e.g. French royal chancery → ancien régime → modern French administrative letter; or the Soviet ЄДСД line → post-Soviet RU/UA/EE) and re-coding the same slots at each date, so that the published "modernity = identifier" trend can be separated from a corpus-composition effect.
predicted_observations: `[prediction]`:
S2 (identifier) presence rises within at least two of three sampled lineages — the "modernity" claim survives the control.
S12 (authentication) stays present at every date in every lineage while its *form* changes (seal → signature → digital) — slot persists, realisation migrates.
Surface slots (S4 authority-mark, S8 subject) vary more *within* lineages than stem slots do, reproducing the atlas's stem/surface split diachronically rather than cross-sectionally.

`[prediction]`: Within-lineage S2 flat or noisy while the cross-sectional trend persists would make "modernity = identifier" an artefact of bin composition; stem slots swinging wildly within a single lineage would weaken the "six centuries, same stem" claim.
uncertainties: `[assumption]`:
Each chosen lineage yields ≥4 datable specimens standardised enough to code (the corpus already anchors French, Islamicate, Soviet, Chinese and Ethiopian lines).
Historical specimens can be coded with the same slot definitions as modern standards (shared with P01-1).
The panel can be written as new analysis in separate files without mutating the frozen `requisites.csv` (the gate must keep passing).

`[assumption]`: Specimen-level dating may require reading fonds rather than standards, and one lineage may be too thinly documented for four points; sample will skew to lineages whose languages I read; ~4 weeks; no participants, no ethics review.

ideas.statement: Extend the atlas's chronology from c. 1412 back to antiquity by coding a small sample of early administrative record objects (cuneiform accounts, Egyptian hieratic dockets, Chinese bronze/bamboo administrative texts, Roman tabulae) on the 14 slots, and use the result to convert the currently qualitative khipu/wampum boundary into an explicit slot-count threshold for what counts as a "document regime".
predicted_observations: `[prediction]`:

Origin (S3), temporal (S5) and authority/authenticate marks (S4/S12) appear in most early administrative objects; identifier (S2) and destination (S6) appear rarely or in recognisably different form (seal-cylinder impression rather than number line).

A non-trivial share of early objects fall *below* the stem threshold, looking more like the khipu than like a charter — i.e. the boundary is a continuum, not a line, and modern "document" is one end of it.
The coding forces an explicit decision about whether impressed seals count as S12; if they do, "authentication is the most universal slot" gains the deepest possible support.

`[prediction]`: Early objects routinely filling the full stem (S12 + S10/S11 + S3/S5) would push the deep grammar back millennia and defeat the continuum expectation; inability to code the objects at all would show the slot vocabulary is *not* medium-neutral and would indict the boundary claim rather than the stem.
uncertainties: `[assumption]`:
Open translations and museum/edition catalogues suffice to code slots without philological specialisation (no assumption of reading cuneiform; coded from published renderings).
The slot vocabulary is medium-neutral — already assumed for the scroll and the knotted cord, but clay/bamboo will push it further.
~20–40 objects across ≥3 traditions are codeable by one person in weeks, not years.

`[assumption]`: Highest philological risk of the six; restriction to objects with published translations skews the sample toward the best-published traditions (Mesopotamia/Egypt) and away from East/South Asia; risk of anachronistic coding of "authentication" on clay; ~4–6 weeks; no participants, no ethics review.

predicted_observations: (P1) Bin A yields S6+S9 co-occurrence recurring in ≥2 traditions, falsifying the fork's universality and yielding a scoped claim: the fork is a property of modern codified genre separation, not of the deep grammar — the disconfirmation threshold and per-tradition analysis frozen exactly as R01 demanded of P01-1. (P3) Bin C (only if reached) shows document-level co-occurrence rates above the system-aggregated zero, quantifying how much the fork was an artefact of system-level aggregation.

Bin A — the bin the recorded evidence directly supports — returns zero co-occurrence across ≥30 specimens and ≥3 traditions under the frozen rule: the fork survives its strongest documented attack, the "evidence wave converted this into a directional test" premise fails, and bins B–C are not worth their sourcing weeks.

(A2) The frozen decision rule separates protocol openings / basmala-doʿā formulas from normative recitals, pre-empting R01's "vocabulary drift, not a rule violation" alternative. (A3) Coding is per specimen (document-level unit) — that is precisely what jointly answers P02-2's aggregation critique.
